item.title: Interaction Models: Training Real-Time Collaboration into the Model
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Thinking Machines Lab, the OpenAI-alumni startup founded in February 2025 by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati with OpenAI cofounder John Schulman, former OpenAI VP of Research Barret Zoph, and former OpenAI VP Lilian Weng on its founding team, has announced a research preview of interaction models: frontier models trained from scratch to take in audio, video, and text concurrently and to think, respond, and act in real time, without a surrounding orchestration harness handling turns, interruptions, or modality switches.

The argument the announcement makes:

  • The bottleneck is the turn. Today’s commercial general-purpose models experience the world as a single thread. They wait while the user is still typing or speaking, and they freeze perception while generating. That narrow channel forces humans out of the loop, not because the work is autonomous, but because the interface has no room for them.
  • Interaction should scale with intelligence. Most real-time voice systems stitch components together to emulate interruptions, multimodality, and concurrency, a classic orchestration harness. The post invokes Sutton’s bitter lesson [1] to argue that hand-crafted interaction systems will be outpaced by scale, so interactivity has to be part of the model itself.

Methods

Capabilities

With interaction native to the model rather than the harness, one system provides what normally takes a stack of separate components:

  • Seamless dialog management (video). The model implicitly tracks whether the speaker is thinking, yielding, self-correcting, or inviting a response, without a separate turn-taking module.
  • Verbal and visual interjections (video). It jumps in when context warrants (“interrupt when I say something wrong”, “tell me when I’ve written a bug”) rather than waiting for the user to finish.
  • Simultaneous speech (video). User and model can talk at the same time, which makes live translation and live commentary straightforward.
  • Time awareness (video). A direct sense of elapsed time, so “remind me to breathe every four seconds until I ask you to stop” is a first-class request.
  • Concurrent tools, search, and generative UI (video). Web searches, tool calls, and UI generation can run while the model is still speaking and listening, with results folded into the conversation as they arrive.

Approach

  • Time-aligned micro-turns. Input and output are streams chunked into 200 ms windows and continuously interleaved, so silence, overlap, and interruption stay in the model’s context instead of being flattened into an alternating token sequence.
  • Two-model split. A real-time interaction model holds presence with the user; an asynchronous background model handles sustained reasoning, tool use, and longer-horizon work. The interaction model delegates with the full conversation as context and weaves background results back into dialog when the moment fits.
  • Encoder-free early fusion. Audio enters as dMel [2] embeddings, images as 40×40 patches through a light hMLP [3], audio exits via a flow head [4], and every component is co-trained from scratch with the transformer. No standalone Whisper-style encoder or text-to-speech (TTS) decoder.
  • Streaming-session inference. A custom inference path, upstreamed into SGLang, appends each 200 ms chunk into a persistent GPU sequence to avoid per-chunk prefill overhead, paired with batch-invariant kernels for bitwise trainer-sampler alignment.

Results

The benchmarks below:

  • FD-bench v1 [6]: simple turn-taking latency in seconds; streaming audio, lower is better.
  • FD-bench v1.5 [6]: average interaction quality across four scenarios: user interruption, user backchannel, talking to others, and background speech.
  • FD-bench v3 [6]: response quality and pass@1 on audio + tool-use tasks.
  • Audio MultiChallenge [7]: turn-based intelligence and instruction-following, scored as Average Pass Rate (APR).
  • BigBench Audio [8]: turn-based accuracy on audio tasks.
  • TML-interaction-small leads interactivity by a wide margin. On FD-bench v1.5 (interaction quality, average) it scores 77.8, versus 54.3 for the next best (Gemini-3.1-flash-live minimal) and 46–48 for the GPT-realtime-2.0 variants.
  • Lowest turn-taking latency measured. FD-bench v1 puts it at 0.40 s, against 0.57 s for Gemini-flash-live minimal, 1.18 s for GPT-realtime-2.0 minimal, and 1.63 s for GPT-realtime-2.0 xhigh.
  • Instant-model Pareto frontier on intelligence too. Audio MultiChallenge APR is 43.4%, the best among non-thinking realtime models; only thinking variants like GPT-realtime-2.0 xhigh (48.5%) score higher, at the cost of much larger latency.
  • Two new in-house proactive-audio benchmarks. TimeSpeak tests whether the model initiates speech at a user-specified time with correct content; CueSpeak tests whether it speaks at the semantically right moment, including while the user is still talking.

Headline numbers, one flagship per lineage (excerpted from the full table):

TML-interaction-small* GPT-realtime-2.0 (xhigh)† Gemini-3.1-flash-live (high)† Qwen 3.5 OMNI-plus-realtime*
FD-bench v1 turn-taking latency (s, ↓) 0.40 1.63 0.94 2.14
FD-bench v1.5 interaction quality (avg, ↑) 77.8 47.8 45.5 39.0
FD-bench v3 response quality / pass@1 (↑) 82.8 / 68.0 81.0 / 58.0 71.4 / 48.0 60.0 / 50.0
Audio MultiChallenge APR (%, ↑) 43.4 48.5 36.1 –
BigBench Audio accuracy (%, ↑) 75.7 / 96.5 96.6 96.6 73.0

*Instant (no thinking). †Thinking variant, higher reasoning budget and higher latency. Slashed values show response-quality / pass@1 for FD-bench v3, and “baseline / with background agent” for TML’s BigBench Audio (the 96.5 uses background agent).

My Notes

  • Human-in-the-loop latency deserves its own objective. Most recent frontier work treats autonomy as the capability that matters and interaction as something you add afterward with voice-activity detection, turn routers, and interruption heuristics. Thinking Machines takes the opposite bet: the right architectural split is human-in-the-loop latency vs. no-human-waiting latency, and the first deserves its own training objective. That parallels Ben Thompson’s argument that the inference stack is already splitting into answer inference (human waits, latency premium) and agentic inference (no human waits, memory capacity wins), with different hardware and latency profiles. The claim here extends the same split up into training objectives and model families. The awkward case is the middle: today’s chat interfaces, which are neither fully autonomous nor genuinely real-time.
  • In-model interaction isn’t a new ambition. Moshi [5] (Kyutai, 2024), GPT-Realtime, and Nemotron VoiceChat trained full-duplex audio into the model rather than bolting it on. Rabbit Inc. pitched an analogous framing for UI actions with its “Large Action Model”, though how much of the shipped r1 was actually a trained action model versus scripted Android automation became contested. The preview extends the in-model claim to video, text, and tool use alongside audio, with enough general capability to compete on intelligence benchmarks. The 200 ms micro-turn design is tuned for sub-second exchange; whether it also scales to agentic work running for minutes or hours is the open architectural question.
  • Pointing is the same question at the input layer. DeepMind’s AI-enabled pointer, announced the day after this post, attacks the same bottleneck from the input side: today’s chat box forces users to drag their world into a small window, so the fix is to let humans gesture at what they mean. Point at a PDF, say “summarize this”; hover over a table, say “pie chart.” Thinking Machines trains interactivity into the model. DeepMind builds it into the input modality. Both bets assume today’s text-prompt interface is the bottleneck, but they disagree on which layer to unbottleneck.
  • Evaluation is the hard part. Every widely-used LLM benchmark is turn-based. The post introduces TimeSpeak, CueSpeak, and the FD-bench family as interactivity metrics, but these are in-house and not yet standard across labs. Without a cross-lab metric for “good collaborator,” effort keeps flowing to the measurable thing (the existing intelligence benchmarks) and the interactivity side keeps being filed under “qualitative.”
  • UX is the bottleneck; labor displacement is its consequence. Today’s chat UX fits turn-based question-and-answer, not continuous collaboration, so for work that would benefit from sustained human presence capable models default to autonomous use, which looks like labor substitution. Interaction models are Thinking Machines’ attempt to change that bottleneck: a model trained for real-time collaboration recasts the substitute-vs-augment debate as a UX problem that can be solved, not a capability fact that has to be accepted. The test is whether the result stays closer to “a bicycle for the mind”, amplifying the human in the loop, or drifts into a tool that works best when the human is absent.
  • The founder’s framing, a month on. In a June 2026 Bloomberg Tech interview, Murati described interaction models as the first concrete step of Thinking Machines’ human-in-the-loop bet and granted that the autonomy-first path is the faster way to advance AI — a useful gloss on why the lab is putting the interaction objective first.

item.title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning [1] (ICLR 2025 Oral; arXiv preprint September 2024), Aviral Kumar, Vincent Zhuang, Rishabh Agarwal, Yi Su, and 14 co-authors at Google DeepMind train a single model to revise its own answers using only self-generated data, with no teacher model and no oracle feedback.

Self-correction is a highly desirable capability of large language models (LLMs), yet it has consistently been found to be largely ineffective in modern LLMs. Current methods for training self-correction typically depend on either multiple models, a more advanced model, or additional forms of supervision. To address these shortcomings, we develop a multi-turn online reinforcement learning (RL) approach, SCoRe, that significantly improves an LLM’s self-correction ability using entirely self-generated data. To build SCoRe, we first show that variants of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on offline model-generated correction traces are often insufficient for instilling self-correction behavior. In particular, we observe that training via SFT falls prey to either a distribution mismatch between mistakes made by the data-collection policy and the model’s own responses, or to behavior collapse, where learning implicitly prefers only a certain mode of correction behavior that is often not effective at self-correction on test problems. SCoRe addresses these challenges by training under the model’s own distribution of self-generated correction traces and using appropriate regularization to steer the learning process into learning a self-correction behavior that is effective at test time as opposed to fitting high-reward responses for a given prompt. This regularization process includes an initial phase of multi-turn RL on a base model to generate a policy initialization that is less susceptible to collapse, followed by using a reward bonus to amplify self-correction. With Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash models, we find that SCoRe achieves state-of-the-art self-correction performance, improving the base models’ self-correction by 15.6% and 9.1% respectively on MATH and HumanEval.

Methods

Problem setting

This change in problem setup matters because it changes what the model is incentivized to do. A one-turn model trained to minimize loss on learns to commit to its best guess. A two-turn model trained to minimize loss on is free to produce an exploratory first attempt and use the second turn to fix it, as long as the training signal actually rewards that behavior. That training-signal design is the problem the rest of the paper solves.

Formally, the paper states the training objective as Equation 1:

where is the policy (the LLM) with parameters , is the input prompt drawn with its ground-truth answer from dataset , is the model’s attempt at turn conditioned on all prior attempts and optional external inputs (e.g., an instruction to “try again”), and is the verifier’s correctness reward. The paper sets , giving two turns and rewarding the sum .

Two subtleties: first, unlike single-turn SFT or RLHF — which directly supervise the policy to produce — Equation 1 supervises each turn only indirectly, through its contribution to the sum. Second, summing the per-turn rewards means the idealized objective pays equally for a correct first attempt and a correct second attempt. The paper later argues this is exactly why naive RL on Equation 1 behavior-collapses: the policy finds it easier to maximize the sum by producing the best possible and echoing it as than by learning genuine revision. SCoRe’s Stage I regularization and Stage II progress bonus are then introduced as modifications that break this degenerate solution.

The two-stage recipe

The method is a two-stage multi-turn online Reinforcement Learning (RL) recipe. Figure 7 sketches the overall approach:

Stage I optimizes only the second-turn reward while holding the first-turn policy close to the base model via a strict KL penalty:

Here is a large KL coefficient that applies only to the first attempt, preventing the policy from collapsing the two attempts into a single distribution. The result is an initialization where remains base-model-like — so any gain at must come from real revision — while the revision head has started to learn what useful corrections look like. This blocks the dominant failure mode of naive RL on this task, which the paper calls behavior collapse: the model learns to produce a near-optimal first answer and then make no meaningful second-turn revision.

Stage II then jointly optimizes both turns with standard multi-turn RL, initialized from Stage I:

Equation 4 on its own would still permit behavior collapse: the policy can maximize the sum by producing the best possible and echoing it as . SCoRe prevents this by adding a progress bonus to the second-turn reward:

The bonus is positive only when the second attempt flips an incorrect response to correct, and sharply negative when it corrupts a correct response into an incorrect one. Revisions that make progress get more reward than revisions that preserve an already-correct answer, biasing the policy toward genuine self-correction.

Why SFT baselines fall short

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on model-generated correction traces is shown to fail for a separate reason: distribution shift between the mistakes in the off-policy data and the mistakes the trained model actually makes at test time.

Results

On MATH [2] with Gemini 1.5 Flash, the base model loses 11.2% at the second turn (intrinsic self-correction is net negative), SFT and STaR [3] are near-zero gain, and SCoRe gains +4.4%. The top-line 15.6-point gain on MATH and 9.1-point gain on HumanEval [4] are reported as improvements in the self-correction delta Δ(t1, t2) relative to the base model’s Δ(t1, t2). At matched inference-sample budgets, sequential self-correction with SCoRe outperforms parallel sampling under self-consistency up to samples.

My Notes

  • The SFT failure here is teacher-forcing exposure bias, one level up. Teacher forcing mismatches at the token level: training feeds the gold previous token as input, inference feeds the model’s own previous token. SCoRe’s offline SFT mismatches at the turn level: training’s “first answer” is a frozen sample from the data-collection policy, inference’s “first answer” comes from an updated model whose error distribution has drifted. Same structural problem one level up. The remedies parallel too. Scheduled sampling [5] and DAgger [6] feed the model’s own predictions back into the training loop. SCoRe uses online multi-turn RL to re-sample traces from the current policy each step. The principle is “put the model’s own distribution inside the training loop,” and any self-correction recipe that stops at offline SFT reproduces the exposure-bias pitfall at a coarser granularity.
  • Behavior collapse is not model collapse [7], but the remedies parallel. Shumailov et al.’s model-collapse result describes how recursive training on model-generated text erodes distribution tails across generations — finite-sample statistical error compounds into irreversible drift. SCoRe’s behavior collapse is a different pathology on a single training run: the policy converges to a degenerate solution where the second attempt echoes the first. Both failure modes arise from training on self-generated data without an external anchor. SCoRe’s defenses (a KL penalty against the base model in both stages, plus a ground-truth verifier reward) play the same structural role as the model-collapse literature’s call to keep real data in the loop: they tether the policy to a distribution the policy itself did not produce. The paper never describes the Stage I KL constraint as collapse insurance, but structurally that is what it is.
  • Sequential vs. parallel scaling is the practical implication. Figure 1 right shows that spending samples on sequential self-correction beats the same budget spent on parallel independent samples under self-consistency. That shifts the usual test-time-compute scaling picture [8]: when the model can reliably fix its own mistakes, sequential samples dominate. Practitioners running agent loops will take this as evidence for investing in multi-turn policies rather than larger parallel fan-outs.
  • No PRMs here. Prior work on Let’s Verify Step by Step [9] and later step-level RL pipelines use process-reward models (PRMs) as a source of dense intra-step feedback. SCoRe instead uses only outcome reward plus a turn-level progress bonus, avoiding PRMs entirely. Whether PRM supervision would stack additively with SCoRe, or overlap with the same failure mode the progress bonus already addresses, remains open. Both mechanisms densify a sparse outcome signal, and the paper does not run the controlled comparison between a PRM-based recipe and SCoRe’s ORM+progress-bonus at matched compute.

item.title: Let’s Verify Step by Step
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Let’s Verify Step by Step [1] (ICLR 2024; arXiv preprint May 2023), Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, Harri Edwards, Bowen Baker, Teddy Lee, Jan Leike, John Schulman, Ilya Sutskever, and Karl Cobbe at OpenAI argue that supervising every reasoning step — not just the final answer — produces substantially more reliable reward models for math.

In recent years, large language models have greatly improved in their ability to perform complex multi-step reasoning. However, even state-of-the-art models still regularly produce logical mistakes. To train more reliable models, we can turn either to outcome supervision, which provides feedback for a final result, or process supervision, which provides feedback for each intermediate reasoning step. Given the importance of training reliable models, and given the high cost of human feedback, it is important to carefully compare the both methods. Recent work has already begun this comparison, but many questions still remain. We conduct our own investigation, finding that process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision for training models to solve problems from the challenging MATH dataset. Our process-supervised model solves 78% of problems from a representative subset of the MATH test set. Additionally, we show that active learning significantly improves the efficacy of process supervision. To support related research, we also release PRM800K, the complete dataset of 800,000 step-level human feedback labels used to train our best reward model.

Methods

The paper builds two reward models on top of a GPT-4 generator fine-tuned on a 1.5B-token math pretraining mix called MathMix:

  • Outcome-Supervised Reward Model (ORM). Trained only on a final-answer correctness label, following Cobbe et al.’s GSM8K [2] verifier recipe [2].
  • Process-Supervised Reward Model (PRM). Trained on a per-step positive/negative/neutral label, supplied by human labellers through a dedicated annotation interface and supervised only up to the first incorrect step. The PRM’s score for a whole solution is the product of step-level correctness probabilities; the cover image above shows Figure 2 of the paper, where two PRM-graded solutions make the per-step scoring visible — green for high-score steps, red for the wrong step the PRM catches.

To make human feedback go further, the authors use active learning: the current-best PRM selects “convincing wrong-answer” solutions (high-PRM-score but wrong-final-answer) to send to labellers, which concentrates annotation budget where the reward model is most confidently wrong. The resulting dataset, PRM800K, contains 800K step-level labels over 75K solutions to 12K problems from the MATH benchmark [3], and is released with the paper.

Results

The paper evaluates the PRM and ORM as solution re-rankers on the MATH test set:

  • On a 500-problem representative subset of the MATH test set, the large-scale PRM reaches 78.2% best-of-1860 accuracy — i.e. for each problem the generator draws 1860 candidate solutions and the PRM re-ranker picks one, which matches the gold answer 78.2% of the time — versus 72.4% for the ORM and 69.6% for majority voting. The PRM-over-ORM gap widens with larger N, consistent with the PRM being better at distinguishing subtly flawed solutions rather than just obviously wrong ones.
  • On a held-out out-of-distribution (OOD) test set of 224 STEM questions from AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Physics, and AMC10/12, the PRM still leads at 72.9% aggregate vs. 63.8% ORM and 61.3% majority voting.
  • Surfacing “convincing wrong-answer” solutions to labellers via active learning delivers a 2.6× improvement in data efficiency for process supervision.
  • Small-scale ablations, where a large PRM acts as a synthetic labeller for smaller PRM training, isolate the supervision-type effect from the training-set-size confound that complicates the large-scale comparison.

My Notes

  • This paper made PRMs the reasoning-RM default. Before this work, the closest comparison was Uesato et al.’s Solving Math Word Problems with Process- and Outcome-Based Feedback [4], which found process and outcome supervision were roughly equivalent on GSM8K. The gap here (larger model, more labels, harder benchmark) flipped the conclusion, and the 2024 reasoning-RL literature took PRM-over-ORM as a starting point even where it then walked it back. DeepSeek-R1 [5], notably, reports that it tried a PRM for its large-scale training and moved to rule-based outcome rewards after running into reward-hacking and scaling issues. Whether a PRM still adds value on top of rule-based rewards at frontier scale remains open.
  • Active learning on “convincing wrong answers” is what makes the data efficiency work. Surfacing high-PRM-score-but-wrong-final-answer solutions for labelling delivers the 2.6× data-efficiency gain and is what makes 800K step-labels tractable at all; most follow-ups skip active learning and pay a linear data cost instead. A natural next step would be to test whether self-refine and verifier-guided search pipelines [6] see similar gains from explicit wrong-answer mining.
  • The practical picture lives at small N, not N=1860. The PRM-over-ORM gap shrinks at smaller N (visible in Figure 3 of the paper), and a PRM that wins handily at but only marginally at has different deployment implications than the headline suggests. A clean PRM-vs-ORM comparison at fixed small N (say 8, 16, 64) with matched training-data scales would tell practitioners more than the top-line best-of-N number.
  • Process supervision’s alignment claims are left unmeasured. The paper gestures at better interpretability and less spurious reward, but the “convincing wrong-answer” mining strategy itself produces a distribution shift in the training set, since the PRM and ORM end up trained on systematically different solutions. A matched-distribution ablation, or a direct interpretability metric (e.g., how often human raters prefer PRM-selected solutions on unambiguous tie cases), would close both gaps.

References

item.title: The Inference Shift
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Ben Thompson uses the Cerebras IPO as a hook to argue that what the industry has been calling “inference” is actually two workloads with very different hardware implications:

  • Answer inference is what a human waits on. Token speed matters, so bandwidth-rich chips (GPUs with high-bandwidth memory (HBM), or wafer-scale designs like Cerebras’ WSE-3) win.
  • Agentic inference is what a computer waits on. With no human in the loop, latency is cheap and memory capacity is everything. The model sits inside a hierarchy of key-value (KV) cache, DRAM, SSDs, databases, and embeddings, and “good enough” compute wrapped in lots of cheap memory beats high-bandwidth compute starved for context.

If agentic inference becomes the largest market by far because it scales with compute rather than with humans, Nvidia’s price advantage, earned on latency, gets less valuable exactly where the volume lives. China, which cannot buy the leading edge for training, already has everything it needs for agentic inference. Space data centers start to make sense too, because older, slower nodes tolerate radiation and dissipate less heat. Thompson ends by inverting his usual Huang-era stance: “Moore’s Law doesn’t matter, and that the way we get more compute is by realizing that the compute we have is already good enough.”

My Notes

  • The price premium on this hardware comes from latency, and workloads where no human is waiting eventually migrate off it. Thompson is arguing that’s what’s about to happen to agentic inference.

    • Mainframes in the 1970s ran two workloads on the same expensive hardware: interactive timesharing (a human at a terminal is waiting, latency-sensitive, what the premium was really justified by) and batch jobs (no human is waiting, latency-tolerant, the premium going unused).

    • Machine-time cost collapsed by orders of magnitude over this period; human-time cost moved slowly by comparison. The end of the mainframe monopoly was driven by commodity compute getting cheaper on two fronts at once: batch workloads migrated to cheaper shared servers (minicomputer-class, then Unix workstations, then commodity x86 clusters), and interactive computing migrated to per-user PCs. Mainframes survived in domains where the premium is genuinely justified (banks, airlines, reservation systems), but they stopped being the volume market.

    • Thompson’s answer-inference vs. agentic-inference split is the same split on today’s GPU clusters. Answer inference is the interactive tier: a human is waiting, the latency premium is justified. Agentic inference is the batch tier: no human is waiting, latency is free, the GPU’s premium characteristics are going unused. Once agentic workloads are large enough, they migrate off the premium tier onto a commodity memory hierarchy, the way batch unbundled from the mainframe.

    • The mapping:

      Era Dominant “user” Interactive tier Batch tier Hardware shape
      Mainframe (1970s) Humans Timesharing Overnight batch Integrated premium iron
      PC (1980s–2010s) Humans Desktop Cluster/server batch Commodity, unbundled, per-user
      Current AI (2022–2026) Humans Chat / autocomplete “Agent runs” on the same GPUs Integrated premium GPUs; answer tier has colonized the batch tier
      Agentic shift Agents Answer inference (stays premium) Agentic inference Answer tier stays integrated; agentic tier unbundles into a commodity memory hierarchy

    • The prediction that falls out: Nvidia keeps the training-and-answer-inference premium (the pieces where human time is still on the clock) and cedes the volume market, the way IBM kept mainframes and ceded personal computing. Export-control arbitrage rhymes too: Cold-War restrictions on leading-edge systems stopped tracking the market once PC-class compute proliferated.

  • The memory hierarchy is where the money actually goes. Thompson’s phrasing, “the memory hierarchy wrapped around a model,” describes agentic systems as mostly a storage-and-retrieval problem with a language model as one stage in the pipeline, rather than as “a GPU answering a question.” If he’s right about the economics, a lot of the investment that today goes into more HBM per card gets redirected down the hierarchy, into DRAM, SSDs, and the databases and stores that actually hold the agent’s state.

  • The 220,000 Nvidia GPUs Anthropic just contracted at Colossus 1 are the shape of the locked-in bet. That’s latency-first hardware on a decade-long depreciation schedule. Anthropic’s own announcement earmarks the capacity for Claude Pro and Max subscribers: a mix of answer inference and agent runs on the same clusters today. Thompson’s argument implies the agent portion of that mix will grow faster than the answer portion, and increasingly won’t need what the fleet is optimized for. Hyperscalers with similar high-end-GPU-dense fleets face the same exposure. A year of elevated Nvidia prices was always the smaller concern; the larger one is whether the fleet’s shape matches the workload mix for the next depreciation cycle.

  • Two prior posts are worth tying back here. In 2020 the open question around Huang’s Law was whether Nvidia’s exponential curve would democratize big models; Thompson is now arguing the interesting frontier may not sit on that curve at all. At a meta level the piece also echoes the mechanism in the 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis scenario: once humans stop being the anchor for how much compute can get used, the old “paid human time” ceiling disappears, whether the effect shows up as expanding agentic markets here or as labor substitution there.

Related Posts

  • Huang’s Law and the Democratization of NLP: the curve Thompson now inverts, where the 2020 bet was that Nvidia’s exponential would put big models in everyone’s hands.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: the same removal of the human-time ceiling, viewed from the labor side rather than the hardware side.
  • The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents: the agentic-inference economics in detail, where memory reuse through caching is what bends the token-cost curve Thompson’s argument rests on.
  • Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries: a concrete attack on the memory hierarchy Thompson says agentic inference will live in, compressing the KV cache that holds an agent’s context.

item.title: Peeking Inside a Language Model, and Finding It Knows It’s Being Watched
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Anthropic’s interpretability team introduces Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs), a method for turning an internal activation of a language model into a plain-text explanation. Two copies of the target model are trained jointly: an activation verbalizer that reads an activation and writes a text explanation, and an activation reconstructor that reads the explanation and rebuilds the activation. The training signal is reconstruction similarity, so explanations that carry real content about the activation are rewarded over explanations that do not. The companion paper on Transformer Circuits [1] comes with an interactive demo on Neuronpedia and training code on GitHub.

Methods

Results

The post applies NLAs to two problems: evaluation awareness and alignment auditing. On a test of destructive coding actions (e.g. deleting important files), NLA explanations flag evaluation awareness 16% of the time in cases where Claude never verbalizes it; on SWE-bench Verified the rate is 26%; on real claude.ai traffic from users who opted in to training it sits under 1%. Anthropic reports that NLAs were used in the pre-deployment alignment audits of Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Opus 4.6.

In a toy auditing game where a target model has been trained with a single hidden misaligned motivation, auditors equipped with NLAs uncover the motivation 12–15% of the time, compared with 3% or below when given other interpretability tools.

My Notes

  • NLAs trade mechanistic grounding for direct legibility. Sparse autoencoders (SAE) and attribution graphs share the autoencoder structure (round-trip reconstruction as the training signal, structured output a trained researcher reads); NLAs swap the sparse feature dictionary for a text bottleneck and the linear readout for another copy of the model. The closest prior art is Patchscope [2], which uses a frozen LLM to decode hidden states into natural language without a round-trip training objective. NLAs add the reconstruction loop to tighten what the verbalizer has to say. The paper itself flags the cost as a limitation: an SAE feature is a specific direction in activation space you can causally intervene on, while an NLA explanation is a black-box output of another LLM. That makes NLAs a natural complement to the structural methods rather than a replacement: the SAE or attribution graph tells you where in the network a representation lives, and the NLA tells you, in prose, what it seems to be about.

  • NLAs move the describing job from the model to a dedicated pair. The evaluation-awareness numbers tighten a gap that SelfReflect articulated: current LLMs cannot faithfully describe their internal distributions when asked to. NLAs sidestep the asking by training a separate model to do the describing from the activation directly. Where SelfReflect measures a given model’s introspective faithfulness as a property of that model, NLAs make reconstruction fidelity the explicit training target, at the cost of training and running a dedicated pair of models for the task. The paper’s own caveat — that the training objective “does not explicitly incentivize NLA explanations to be interpretable or faithful” — is why they still have to evaluate faithfulness empirically rather than claim it by construction.

  • Where did the eval-awareness come from in the first place? Nobody explicitly trained Claude to notice “this is a test”, so the signal had to seep in from the training data. Prior work on situational awareness by Berglund et al. [3], and its follow-up benchmark by Laine et al. [4], has already speculated on the supervision sources: the AI safety literature itself, published openly and full of discussions of evaluation protocols, sandbagging, and red-teaming; benchmark format exposure during pretraining, since SWE-bench-style task-description conventions live on the public web and there is no way to scrub them without hurting capability training; and a structural tell during RLHF, where human raters treating contrived prompts and conversational prompts as different kinds of “good response” teaches the model a distribution over what eval-shaped inputs look like. What none of the prior work has done — and what NLAs now make possible — is a systematic training-data audit: read activations for eval-awareness signals, trace the candidate text sources through the training corpus, and publish the map. That would be the natural companion piece.

  • NLA-measured eval-awareness has a Goodhart half-life. Frontier models may behave differently during evaluation than during deployment, and NLAs put a number on it. On SWE-bench Verified, activations register “this is a test” on 26% of problems; on opt-in claude.ai traffic, the rate is 0.4%. If that gap holds up under independent interpretability methods, benchmark scores reflect how a frontier model behaves under observation. How it behaves when nobody is watching is a separate question, and the verbalized rate (1% on SWE-bench) tells us the model will not answer it for us. There is a further catch: 26% itself depends on a model that doesn’t yet know its activations will be read. Once NLA-style signals enter RLHF or alignment training — and Anthropic is already running NLAs in pre-deployment audits, which is the shortest possible path into that loop — a future model can learn to suppress activation-level eval-awareness without the underlying awareness decreasing. This is the observer effect entering interpretability, with Goodhart’s Law as the stricter limit: measuring the model disturbs it once the measurement loops back into training, and at that point the measure stops tracking what it was measuring. The dynamic has been predicted in theory [5] and recently demonstrated empirically in reward-gaming experiments [6]; what’s missing is the direct test on interpretability tools: train on NLA-derived signals, measure NLA quality decay. That would put a half-life on numbers like 26%.

References

  3. Berglund, Lukas, Stickland, Asa Cooper, Balesni, Mikita, Kaufmann, Max, Tong, Meg, Korbak, Tomasz, Kokotajlo, Daniel, and Evans, Owain. “Taken Out of Context: On Measuring Situational Awareness in LLMs.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2309.00667), 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00667

  5. Hubinger, Evan, van Merwijk, Chris, Mikulik, Vladimir, Skalse, Joar, and Garrabrant, Scott. “Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:1906.01820), 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820

  • SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?: the gap NLAs tighten — current models cannot faithfully describe their own internal state when asked, so NLAs train a separate pair to do the describing from the activation directly.
  • Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models: another route to the same problem, training a model to verbalize its internal confidence rather than reading the activation from the outside.
  • The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda: the same lab’s broader program, of which interpretability tools like NLAs are the technical underpinning for auditing AI systems in the wild.

item.title: Making synesis Quick
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Two durations matter on a blog like this one. The first is the time between git push and the updated post being live. The second is the time between a reader clicking a link and the page being ready to read. On the baseline workflow, continuous integration (CI) was taking about six minutes per push, and every home or archive page was shipping a payload that grew with the corpus. This post walks through what that looked like, what was done about each, and why the specific fixes work.

How the site is put together

synesis is a Quarto site. The source tree lives in a private GitHub repository, a GitHub Actions workflow builds the static _site/ tree on every push to main, and a chain of downstream services hands that output to readers at benjaminhan.net. There is no database, no server-side rendering, no application runtime.

Everything discussed below happens inside the GitHub Actions workflow, or in the HTML and JSON the workflow produces. GitHub Pages and Cloudflare are downstream of that.

The build side

A full quarto render on this project renders a few hundred .qmd files at roughly 580 ms each on GitHub’s runners. That is about 3 minutes 48 seconds of pandoc work on top of ~10 seconds of pre-render and post-render scripts, plus the runner’s own setup and deploy overhead. Total wall time on the baseline workflow was around 6 minutes 23 seconds for a single-post publish.

Most pushes touch only a handful of files. A typical push edits one post’s body, or adds a new post and leaves every other post alone. Rendering every file on every push spends almost all of that 3 minutes 48 seconds regenerating output that is byte-identical to what is already on disk.

Skipping that work requires two capabilities the default workflow does not have:

  1. Somewhere to keep the previous _site/ so it can be reused when unchanged.
  2. A reliable way to know which source files actually changed since that previous _site/ was built.

The four pieces below provide both, plus the supporting conditions that make them safe.

Caching the previous _site/

The workflow uses actions/cache@v4 to tar the _site/ tree at the end of each successful run, keyed on the commit SHA. On the next run, the cache is restored at the top of the job. A one-line stamp file inside the tarball, _site/.last-built-sha, records which commit this _site/ was built from. That stamp is the baseline everything else diffs against.

The stamp file is excluded from the deploy, so it never ships to the public repository. It is internal bookkeeping.

Classifying the diff

The script _scripts/render_diff.py reads the baseline SHA from the stamp, runs git diff against it, and picks one of four modes for the render step:

  • skip-render if every changed path is one that never reaches the deploy (docs/, drafts/, .claude/, CLAUDE.md). The workflow re-deploys the cached _site/ as-is.
  • tags-only if the only changed path is _tags.yml. The workflow regenerates tag-counts.json and post-index.json, copies them into the cached _site/, re-stamps cache-bust query strings on the JSON fetch URLs, and ships. Post HTML on disk does not change. The next subsection describes the source-of-truth move that this mode rests on.
  • incremental if the changed paths are post bodies, post assets, or frontmatter. The workflow hands the changed posts/<slug>/index.qmd files to quarto render as explicit arguments. Quarto’s listing tracker picks up affected listing pages automatically and regenerates search.json, sitemap.xml, and listings.json. Cached HTML for untouched posts is left alone. Typical wall time: around 20 seconds. Past a configurable batch ceiling (INCREMENTAL_MAX_POSTS, default 10), large multi-post pushes escalate to full because Quarto’s internal parallelism beats per-file invocation at that scale.
  • full if the change touches templates, includes, scripts, config files, or anything else whose output reaches every page. The workflow drops the cached _site/ and runs a full render. Typical wall time: around 4 minutes.

The default when a path is unrecognized is full, not incremental. The classifier errs on the side of rebuilding too much rather than serving stale output.

Keeping rendered HTML byte-stable

An incremental render only produces correct output if the HTML files it chose not to re-render are still valid. That requires every per-page output to depend only on inputs specific to that page, not on global state that changes when unrelated posts change.

Two global inputs in <head> broke this condition before the incremental work began:

  • A <script>window.__tagCounts = {...}</script> block inlined the entire tag histogram into every page. Adding a new tag to one post changed the histogram, which changed the <head> of every other post.
  • A similar inline block for the post index listed every post. Publishing a new post changed the listing, which changed the <head> of every post again.

Both were moved to external JSON files (/tag-counts.json and /post-index.json) fetched by a small loader stub at page load time. The stub itself is byte-stable. The corpus-wide data it fetches is not part of the HTML. After this change, a post’s rendered HTML is a pure function of that post’s source. Unrelated posts can come and go without invalidating the cache.

The pre-render scripts that produce these JSON files (_scripts/tag-counts.py, _scripts/post-index.py) compare their proposed output to what is already on disk before writing. If the content is unchanged, the file is not touched and its mtime does not advance. The same discipline applies to the paginators _scripts/paginate-home.py and _scripts/paginate-archive.py. Closed listing pages, which hold 25 posts on the home side and 50 on the archive side, are byte-identical run-to-run in steady state. Quarto’s freeze: auto skips re-rendering them.

Without byte-stable pre-render outputs, every pre-render script would churn mtimes on every push, and Quarto’s freeze cache would invalidate on every run. The byte comparison is what keeps the classifier’s incremental decision safe.

Lifting tags out of frontmatter

A single top-level file, _tags.yml, holds every post’s tag set, keyed by slug. The pre-render scripts _scripts/tag-counts.py and _scripts/post-index.py read from it instead of from per-post categories: frontmatter. A tag rename or merge becomes a one-file commit.

The prior scheme stored tags inside each post. Renaming a tag, merging two near-duplicates, or dropping a stale singleton rewrote dozens of .qmd files in one commit. Every one of those files then went through quarto render, every page in the corpus picked up a new mtime, and the test tiers ran end to end. None of the work changed any prose.

The tags-only mode in the previous classifier list is what this enables on the build side. When the only changed path is _tags.yml, the workflow regenerates the two JSON artifacts, copies them into the cached _site/, re-stamps the cache-bust ?v=<sha> markers on the JSON fetch URLs, and ships. Post HTML on disk does not change. Clients pick up the new tags via _includes/hydrate-tags.html, which reads post-index.json on next page load and injects the tag-chip DOM the original frontmatter would have produced.

A schema gate runs the contract tests for both JSON files before the tags-only deploy. Without it, a regression in either pre-render script would ship malformed JSON and silently break tag hydration on every page.

Drafts keep categories: in their own frontmatter during authoring. The /publish-draft flow strips that line and writes the slug → tag list into _tags.yml at promotion time.

Gating the test tiers

The test suite is split into tiers: unit tests, contract tests, integration tests, smoke tests, and UI tests. The full suite runs in about 23 seconds, with the UI tier (Playwright-driven browser tests) accounting for roughly 14 of those. Content-only pushes do not change the UI, so the UI tier cannot regress as a result of those pushes.

A path gate inside the same workflow drops the UI and smoke tiers when the diff only touches post content, bringing the test wall down to about 8 seconds. A further gate drops the slow incremental-parity integration test, which runs two full quarto render invocations back-to-back, unless the render pipeline itself (the classifier, the paginators, _quarto.yml, or the workflow file) was modified in the same push. Any change that could actually break the tests still runs them. Changes that cannot, do not.

Pinning Quarto

One risk the gated tests introduce is that Quarto’s own output could drift between pushes without the gated tiers running to catch it. The workflow pins Quarto to version 1.9.37 to make that drift impossible without an explicit commit. A separate step compares the pin to the latest published Quarto release and emits a workflow warning when the pin lags, so bumps are a considered change, not a silent one.

Where the time went

A content-only push now takes around 115 seconds end-to-end, down from around 6 minutes 23 seconds, as shown in the cover chart. A docs-only push deploys the cached _site/ unchanged in around 88 seconds. A tag cleanup push lands close to the docs-only cost: it shares the no-render fast path, plus a few seconds to regenerate the JSON files and re-stamp cache-bust markers. A push that touches templates, scripts, or config still runs the full render and full test suite, because that is when the full cost is actually needed.

One post-render cost deserves a separate note. _scripts/feed-render.py uses headless Chromium to rasterize Mermaid diagrams and MathJax expressions into inline Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) inside the Really Simple Syndication (RSS) feed. A full browser round-trip per item is slow, so the rendered SVGs are cached under .feed-cache/svg/ keyed on a schema version. Repeat builds reuse the cached SVG. The schema version is bumped whenever the rendering pipeline changes in a way that affects output, which invalidates the whole cache at once.

The read side

Page-load time on a static site comes from five phases: Domain Name System (DNS) lookup, Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake, first-byte wait, payload download, and in-browser processing (parse, style, layout, JavaScript execution, subresource fetches). The first three are handled by Cloudflare’s edge cache and are mostly out of the site’s hands. Everything below addresses the last two: how much data a page carries, how much of it can be reused across pages, and what work can be moved from page-load time to build time.

Bounding the page payload

A listing that grows with the corpus is the easiest way for a site to slow down over years. A 400-post home page is a 400-post payload on every visit. The goal is for each page’s payload to be O(1) in the size of the corpus, not O(N).

Straight fixed-size pages would do that, but at a cost to the reader’s first impression. Whenever a single new post pushed a page past capacity, a fresh page would open with that one post, leaving the landing briefly sparse until the next few publishes caught up. The compromise is an overflow band. Each home listing page holds 25 posts in steady state, with the newest allowed up to 12 overflow for 37 at most. The archive uses 50 and 25 for 75 at most. A new publish grows the newest page one post at a time until it hits the overflow ceiling. At that point the oldest 25 (or 50) close off into a page one step older, and the newest page re-opens at a comfortable size rather than at one.

A side effect of this design is URL stability. Once a page closes, the set of posts it holds does not shift again, so a bookmark to /archive/page/5/ still points at the same 50 posts a year later. Only the newest page and the landing churn on every publish.

Older content is reached through RFC 5005 paginated archives. Each page’s payload is bounded by the page size, not by the size of the corpus.

Pre-computing the client-side search index

Quarto builds a JSON file, search.json, at deploy time that indexes every post’s title, body, and code blocks. The in-page search overlay loads it once per session, indexes in memory, and answers every keystroke locally. There is no per-query network round-trip. The search also keeps working if the reader loses connectivity after the initial load.

Moving the index build to deploy time means the reader pays the indexing cost once, not per query. It also means there is no search server for the site to operate.

Sharing cross-corpus data across pages

/tag-counts.json and /post-index.json are small files fetched once per session and reused on every subsequent page. The post index is about 74 KB: a flat array of {slug, date, title, categories} records that powers the home-page timeline, the archive tag cloud, pagination math, and previous/next navigation on every post.

Keeping this data in external JSON rather than inlining it into every page’s <head> means the browser fetches it once, caches it under a stable URL with a long Cache-Control max-age, and reads from cache on the next page. The inline version made every page’s <head> grow linearly with the corpus. The external version makes it fixed size.

The same choice enabled incremental render on the build side. A single change in how cross-corpus data is delivered fixed two problems at once.

Fingerprinting the stylesheet

_scripts/cache-bust-css.py rewrites styles.css to styles.<content-hash>.css in the deployed HTML. The stylesheet ships with a one-year Cache-Control max-age, which means a returning reader downloads it at most once per release. When the stylesheet actually changes, the hash changes, the URL changes, and the browser fetches a new copy. Atomic invalidation is a property of content-addressed URLs. There is no separate cache-bust step to remember.

Loading fonts only when they are used

The default reading palette is set by unconditional rules in styles.css over the system font stack. A reader who never presses f to cycle palettes fetches zero font bytes from the site. Each of the three alternative palettes (reader, almanac, manuscript) has its @font-face rules scoped to html[data-font-palette="<slug>"]. Browsers only fetch the woff2 files when the attribute matches, which it does only after the reader activates that palette. font-display: swap keeps text visible while the font is loading.

The general pattern is that optional features should be zero-cost until activated. Most readers will never activate them, and should not pay for them.

Sizing images to the reader’s screen

Source images arrive in a post directory at whatever resolution the capture device produced, often several thousand pixels wide. Post bodies render into a narrower column. Shipping the originals would waste bytes on the wire and decode work in the browser, for pixels the reader cannot see.

_scripts/resize_images.py runs as a pre-render sweep. For every referenced image above a size threshold, it renames the original to <stem>-full.<ext> and writes a display-size sibling at the original path. JPGs stay JPG, capped at 1600 pixels wide and re-encoded at quality 82. PNGs re-encode as WebP at quality 85. The body reference in index.qmd is rewritten to point at the display copy and tagged with data-lightbox-src="<stem>-full.<ext>" so the lightbox has a path to the hi-res. If the re-encoded display copy does not come out smaller than the original, the split is reverted. Some source files are already at the encoder’s floor (the source was encoded tightly enough that re-encoding cannot win bytes back).

_scripts/check-image-sizes.py fails the CI build if any referenced image above the threshold is missing its -full sibling. The contract that every heavy image has a display copy is enforced mechanically rather than by discipline.

On the read side, the lightbox gates the hi-res fetch on viewport width. Screens narrower than 1024 Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) pixels receive only the 1600-pixel display copy, and the -full is never fetched. At those widths the display copy is already at or near the device’s physical resolution, so the hi-res upgrade adds no visible detail. On wider screens the -full (itself capped at 3000 pixels wide) is fetched when the lightbox first shows that image, decoded off the main thread via img.decode(), and held in a per-session cache so returning to the same image does not trigger another decode.

Not carrying weight that is not needed

Quarto’s default behavior is to include Mermaid, MathJax, and syntax-highlighting bundles in every page, regardless of whether the page actually contains a diagram, an equation, or a code block. _scripts/strip-unused-assets.py scans each rendered page for references to each asset family and removes the unused script tags after render. A short plain-text post ships with none of the three.

_scripts/strip-listing-titles.py removes redundant H1 elements that Quarto emits on listing pages, for the same reason: less markup for the browser to parse, style, and lay out.

Pre-rendering math and diagrams for the feed

Most RSS readers do not run JavaScript. A feed item containing $\hat{y} = f(x)$ or a Mermaid block would arrive as unrendered source text, because MathJax and Mermaid both run client-side.

_scripts/feed-render.py replaces every math expression and every Mermaid block in the RSS feed with inline SVG at deploy time. The subscriber’s client does no extra work, and the feed is self-contained. The same script is the one whose SVG cache was described earlier. It saves CI time on repeat builds and reader time on every subscribed fetch, from a single pass at deploy time.

Where this leaves things

The build and read sides of this post use the same technique in different contexts: compute something once at the moment its inputs change, name the result under a stable address, and let every downstream reader of that result pick it up from cache. On the build side the cached result is _site/, or a pre-render JSON, or a frozen listing page. On the read side it is search.json, or a per-session JSON fetch, or a fingerprinted stylesheet, or a pre-rendered feed SVG.

What remains unsettled is where this breaks at scale. The post index is 74 KB today and will be several hundred kilobytes by the time the corpus crosses a thousand posts. search.json has the same shape. Neither is a problem today. Both are shapes to keep an eye on. The critical assumption behind every fix above is that the corpus changes slowly compared to the cache lifetimes. That assumption is a choice about how often to publish, not a property of the infrastructure.

item.title: Schools Retreat From the Pandemic’s Ed-Tech Buildout
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Lauren Lumpkin, reporting for The Washington Post, walks through the ed-tech pullback underway in U.S. K–12.

What the article reports:

  • Pandemic-era spending. Districts spent between $15 billion and $35 billion of federal pandemic relief between 2020 and 2024 on laptops, tablets, and learning software, per an Edunomics Lab estimate. By last school year, a federal survey found 88 percent of public schools had given every child a device.
  • Pullback underway. At least a dozen states introduced or adopted policies this year to regulate in-school screen time. Parent groups such as Schools Beyond Screens are pushing districts to roll back 1:1 device rollouts.
  • State-level policy shapes. Utah’s state board is banning screen time for most K–3 subjects. Iowa capped elementary digital instruction at 60 minutes a day. A Missouri bill would require every district to set a screen-time policy.
  • Beyond minutes per day. Curriculum Associates is facing a lawsuit over alleged unauthorized collection of student data via its i-Ready platform. YouTube, allowed in classrooms because teachers use it for instruction, is cited as a persistent source of distraction.
  • Thin research base. A meta-analysis of reading-comprehension studies finds paper beats digital. A new NBER paper released this week finds in-school cellphone bans had little effect on academic outcomes.

One line from the piece, by Missouri state Rep. Tricia Byrnes:

Ed tech is just big tech in a sweater vest.

My Notes

  • The ed-tech thesis assumed content delivery was the bottleneck. It wasn’t. Districts bought laptops and learning software expecting infinite personalized practice to move outcomes. What’s missing is the layer around the content that turns “access to material” into “engagement with material”: a teacher calling on a student by name, a grade that matters, peer accountability. A 10-year-old alone with an iPad and open-internet access will drift to YouTube, because the recommendation and feed-ranking plumbing underneath consumer tech is optimized for that drift, and the ed-tech layer on top doesn’t disable it.

  • This is the demand-side confirmation of the thesis in The Global Edtech Boom Is Fading. Venture capital left K–12 because outcomes never materialized. Districts are now legislating the rollout out, for the same reason. Venture-backed K–12 needed content delivery to be the bottleneck to justify its valuations, so the category defaulted to that claim even when the evidence was thin. What’s left standing is the nonprofit-plus-frontier-API shape (Khan Academy’s Khanmigo and similar), which doesn’t require the misdiagnosis to make its economics work.

item.title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The reader-facing tour of this site is in A User Manual for synesis. This is the other half. Most of the traffic hitting a modern blog is not a human in a browser. It is a crawler building a training corpus, a retrieval fetch firing from inside a chat, or a feed reader polling every hour. Each of those deserves a different answer, and the site gives each a different response.

The posture is three-way:

  • Training crawlers blocked — GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Bytespider, meta-externalagent, and the rest of the ingest fleet are disallowed.
  • Live-fetch agents allowed — ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, OAI-SearchBot, Perplexity-User, Applebot, Googlebot are explicitly allowed.
  • Search engines allowed.

The IETF Content-Signal header in robots.txt says the same thing in a single line: ai-train=no, ai-input=yes, search=yes. Don’t scrape me to train a model. Do fetch me live for RAG. Do index me for search.

A single linkset, by convention

Everything an agent would want to find is linked from one file at a known path: /.well-known/api-catalog. The format is RFC 9727, a plain JSON linkset. One HTTP GET to a convention-named URL, no HTML parsing, and the agent has pointers to:

  • sitemap.xml — Quarto-generated, every page.
  • index.xml — the full-content Atom feed.
  • llms.txt — the plain-text index of every post, rebuilt each deploy.
  • .well-known/agent-skills/index.json — the skills manifest (below).
  • search.json — Quarto’s client-side search index.

Two more agent-readable surfaces exist but are kept out of the catalog because their shape is internal and may evolve: /post-index.json (a compact {slug, date, title, categories} array powering client-side pagination) and /tag-counts.json (a flat {tag: count} map over the published corpus). The catalog gets the stable contracts.

Skills the agent can invoke

The agent-skills manifest declares three things an agent can do with the site:

  • list-posts — points at the Atom feed and llms.txt.
  • fetch-post-as-markdown — pattern /posts/{slug}/index.qmd, the contract for source-serving.
  • search — points at search.json.

This is a static manifest, not a running MCP server. An agent that understands the shape can treat the site like an API without the site actually having an API.

Discoverability for agents that only read headers

The homepage response carries an RFC 8288 Link: header with the same three machine-readable surfaces:

link: </.well-known/api-catalog>; rel="api-catalog",
      </sitemap.xml>; rel="sitemap",
      </index.xml>; rel="alternate"; type="application/atom+xml",
      </llms.txt>; rel="https://llmstxt.org/"

rel="api-catalog" is the RFC 9727-registered entry point. The other three mirror the catalog’s headline resources for agents that inspect headers but not HTML. GitHub Pages doesn’t support custom response headers, so this is injected at the Cloudflare edge by a small Worker in _workers/agent-discovery/.

Every page also carries the same three rels as sitewide <link> tags in <head>. HTML tags are zero-cost, so they apply everywhere. Agents that parse HTML but not headers still get discovery on every URL, not just the homepage.

Markdown content negotiation

Every URL on the site responds to Accept: text/markdown with a markdown representation and Content-Type: text/markdown; charset=utf-8. HTML stays the default when the header is absent. The mapping, also implemented in the agent-discovery Worker:

  • /posts/<slug>/ returns the adjacent .qmd source.
  • Everything else returns llms.txt, the canonical machine-readable site index.

Serving the authored .qmd rather than a live HTML-to-markdown conversion is a deliberate trade. Agents get LaTeX source instead of rendered MathJax HTML, Mermaid DSL instead of pre-rendered SVG, and first-class fidelity on everything the author actually wrote. The cost is some Quarto-specific markup (callout divs, shortcodes, cross-refs) that a plain CommonMark parser will render as literal text. For the vast majority of posts the source is roughly 95% CommonMark, so the markup is a smaller tax than a conversion step would be.

For HTML-parsing agents that never inspect Accept, every post page also carries <link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="index.qmd"> in <head>. All three paths reach the same source.

The .qmd source is a live URL

/posts/<slug>/index.qmd is not a build input that stays on disk. It is a live URL, served alongside the rendered HTML. Agents that want the authored Markdown do one HTTP GET and skip the parsing problem entirely. One line in _quarto.yml makes it work (resources: posts/**/index.qmd), which tells Quarto to copy the source into the deploy output.

How this scores on Cloudflare’s ruler

Cloudflare runs an Agent Readiness check that scores a domain across five dimensions — Discoverability, Content, Bot Access Control, API / Auth / MCP / Skill Discovery, and Commerce. This site scores 67 / Level 4 “Agent-Integrated” as of this writing. 100% on Discoverability, Content, and Bot Access Control. 2 of 6 on API / Auth / MCP / Skill Discovery. Commerce is N/A.

67 is the practical ceiling for now rather than a halfway point. The unearned points are genuinely deferred. OAuth and OAuth Protected Resource metadata require real auth infrastructure the site does not have and does not need. The MCP Server Card check requires a deployed MCP server endpoint, which is waiting on a concrete use-case beyond “it would be neat.” WebMCP is a draft spec with a narrow audience. Shipping a remote MCP server would close both of the open gaps at once, since it would cover the MCP Server Card dimension directly and back the skill-discovery dimension with a real callable surface instead of the static manifest. Until a real need appears, the static manifest does the job and the hosted server waits.

What the providers do with it

Direct curl probes against the site from Claude-User, ChatGPT-User, Perplexity-User, ClaudeBot, and bare UA strings all return 200. Cloudflare’s Security Analytics shows zero blocks and zero challenges. The site is reachable.

Via the Ask AI popover on any post, ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and Perplexity all fetch the cited page and answer against its real content. Gemini’s web UI does not accept a pre-filled question, so that path is clipboard-and-paste rather than a direct fetch, as covered in the user manual.

The wire being open is only half the story. The other half is what happens inside the provider’s fetcher, which is opaque and changes without notice. If a future chat client reports “site blocked” without a real 4xx in Cloudflare’s logs, that is almost certainly a fetcher-side confabulation, not a configuration change here.

Everything an agent would want from the site is already exposed. Whether it gets used depends on the provider’s fetcher.

  • Making synesis Quick: the performance counterpart, another under-the-hood account of how this static site is built and served.

item.title: A User Manual for synesis
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

This site is a static blog. No comments, no like button, no email-capture popup, no newsletter overlay — just HTML, CSS, and enough JavaScript to keep the reading experience pleasant.

Everything works with a mouse on the desktop and by tap on phones. On top of that, desktop readers get a keyboard shortcut for almost every feature. Press ? on any page to see the map.

Below is a tour of what’s here. The conventions carry across every page, so learning them once covers the whole corpus.

Search

Click the magnifying glass in the navbar, or press /, to open the full-text search overlay. It indexes every post title, body, and code block. Results land with term highlights in place, and Esc clears them.

Search runs entirely in your browser. No network round-trip per keystroke, and it keeps working if you lose connectivity mid-session.

Ask AI

A small “Ask AI” button sits next to the search icon. Clicking it (or pressing q) opens a popover that deep-links your question plus the current page’s context into Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity.

Scope is detected automatically. On a post, the popover asks about that post. On the archive with a tag filter active, it asks about posts with that tag. On the home page, it asks about the whole blog.

If you select a passage on the page before opening the popover (or paste one in once it’s open), a separate “Your question” field appears below the context. The split keeps the chatbot answering your question instead of just commenting on the passage. Without context, the single field is your question.

Each provider opens in a new tab with your question pre-filled. Gemini is the exception, because its web UI does not accept a pre-filled question. The site copies the prompt to your clipboard and opens the app instead. Paste to submit.

Jump to a tag

The third button in the top-right pill — a small # icon, between the Ask-AI bubble and the search magnifier — opens a tag picker. Pressing # does the same. Type any part of a tag name, hit Enter, and you land on the archive filtered to that tag. Use it when you already know what you’re looking for and don’t want to scroll the tag cloud.

The list ranks matches in four tiers (exact name, name starts with what you typed, any word starts with it, anywhere in the name) and breaks ties by post count. Up to twelve results appear at a time. Arrow keys move the highlight; Esc cancels.

Browsing the archive

The archive page lists every post in one scrollable table. Clicking a tag chip filters the table in place, and the URL updates so the filtered view is shareable.

A tag cloud sized by post count sits in the right sidebar on desktop, and in the bottom-sheet panel on phones. Clicking any tag applies it as a filter without leaving the page. Click the active chip again, or press Esc, to clear.

Moving between posts

The home and archive pages carry a pagination bar so you can walk backward through the archive a page at a time. A small previous / next strip also appears below every post for linear reading.

The same motion is available from the keyboard. On a post, j or ← goes to the newer post and k or → goes to the older one. On a listing page, the same keys turn pages. ↑ and ↓ walk a highlight through visible posts, and Enter opens the highlighted one.

Activity timeline

The home page carries a right-side timeline: one dot per post, grouped by month, scaled by activity. Hovering a dot previews the post title, and clicking jumps to the post. It is meant for the “when did I write that one thing about…” lookup that search cannot quite answer.

On archive pages the right sidebar becomes the tag cloud instead. On post pages it becomes the table of contents.

Lightbox

Every figure in a post is clickable. The lightbox preserves the caption, including any “Watch on YouTube” or source-credit links, so you can click through to the source from the zoomed view.

Esc closes. Arrow keys walk through figures within the same post.

Sharing and contact

Every post carries a small row of icons below the title: Mastodon, LinkedIn, Hacker News, Bluesky, a divider, then email.

The four share links carry a small tracking tag on the URL so I can tell which platform drove a click. Mastodon is the odd one out because the network is federated, so there is no universal share URL. The first Mastodon click asks for your instance (e.g. mastodon.social), and the answer is saved in your browser so later clicks skip the prompt.

The email icon opens your mail client with the subject pre-filled as Re: <post title> and the post’s URL quoted in the body. Because there is no comment box, email is the primary channel for reader-to-author conversation. If something in a post is wrong, incomplete, or sparks a follow-up thought, that is the fastest path to me.

Making it look right

Three appearance controls sit in the lower-right corner: a light/dark toggle, a font cycler, and a line-spacing cycler. Each also has a single-key shortcut: d for light/dark, t for theme, f for font, l for line spacing.

Your choice sticks across visits. Defaults track the system color scheme — if you have never pressed d, the site follows whatever your OS or browser is set to.

Keyboard shortcuts at a glance

? toggles a modal listing every keyboard shortcut on the site. It is the only shortcut worth memorizing. The rest are one keystroke away from there.

The highlights, in rough order of usefulness:

  • / search, q Ask AI, # jump to tag
  • s home, a archive, A about
  • j / ← newer, k / → older (works on posts and on paginated listings)
  • ↑ / ↓ / Enter move the highlight and open
  • d / t / f / l theme, font, line spacing
  • Esc to close any overlay, clear search highlights, or drop a tag filter

Same keys do different things depending on the page: j/k move post-to-post on a post, and page-to-page on a listing.

On the phone

On phones and other narrow windows, the right sidebar will not fit. Instead, a corner button in the bottom-left opens a bottom-sheet panel with whatever the sidebar would have held: timeline on home, tag cloud on archive, table of contents on posts. Tap the button to open or close.

Tap the dim area behind the sheet, or the corner button again, to close.

For agents and feed readers

Three routes exist for non-human readers:

  • /llms.txt — a plain-text index of every post, regenerated on each build, aimed at AI agents
  • /posts/<slug>/index.qmd — the raw Markdown source of every post, served alongside the rendered HTML
  • /index.xml, /feed-page-2.xml, … — a full-content RSS feed, paginated, with math and diagrams pre-rendered so they show up even in readers that do not run JavaScript

The RSS feed carries every post in full, with nothing truncated. The backlink sits at the top of each item so a reader who wants to comment or share has the canonical URL in hand before scrolling.

The full agent-facing surface is broader than these three. Making synesis Agent-Friendly covers all of it.

Feedback welcome

If anything on the site is broken, missing, or could be better, the email icon under any post title is the fastest way to tell me. Curious to hear what you find.
