item.title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The Pentagon began releasing its Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) files today, following a February executive order. A government report counts more than 750 new UAP sightings between May 2023 and June 2024. CBS News canvassed six scientists on what they expect to find. The consensus: don’t expect alien technology, expect heavy redaction, and expect the conspiracy frame to survive contact with the documents no matter what they contain.

Sean Kirkpatrick — physicist, first director of AARO (July 2022 – December 2023)

On who will read the release and come away unhappy:

There are going to be unsatisfied people. You’re going to have a bunch of people who are going to continue to cry conspiracy, they’re going to say there’s a cover-up.

He views the release order as “a distraction for the administration.” What AARO actually uncovered, he told CBS, ranged from “hazing” in the Air Force to what he called “deceptions” designed to hide secret defense programs. His office “had to stand up anything they could declassify,” but proof of extraterrestrial life wasn’t there:

Nothing would have made me happier in that job but to have discovered alien technology and rolled it out. I don’t expect to see anything new.

Kirkpatrick believes there’s likely life somewhere in the universe, but “the probability that extraterrestrial intelligent life is here is little to none.”

Federica Bianco — associate professor at the University of Delaware, NASA UAP study team

On the prior:

The probability that we are the only life form or even the only technical society in the universe is negligibly small.

On what the panel has seen so far:

As a scientist and a member of the NASA UAP panel, I haven’t seen anything that indicates that we have observed phenomena that violate the laws of physics and require an alien society visiting us to be explained.

Neil deGrasse Tyson — director of the Hayden Planetarium at the American Museum of Natural History

On what he’ll actually look for in the files:

An actual alien. If one is presented, then no documents are necessary at all.

On what the files may illuminate:

[M]ost people who look at the sky (day or night) are unfamiliar with optical, climactic, and astronomical phenomena. When that’s the case, a person is prone to report mysterious and unidentified objects.

On the jump from “unfamiliar” to “alien”:

The urge to have immediate answers drives many people to explain what they see as visiting space aliens from across the galaxy. I call this, “aliens of our ignorance.”

On why a cover-up is unlikely to hold in the smartphone era:

Billions of photos and a million hours of video are uploaded daily to the internet, and none of them contain images of actual aliens. […] The implicit assumption is that the government (somehow) has access to visiting aliens that no one else in the world with a smart phone has. And that the government has successfully kept it a secret among hundreds and possibly thousands of people. All the while, forgetting Benjamin Franklin’s edict, “Three people can keep a secret if two of them are dead.”

From the prologue of his forthcoming book, Take Me To Your Leader: Perspectives on Your First Alien Encounter:

In science, skepticism is foundational to our profession, so we uphold standards of evidence that some interpret as disinterest or even denial. Don’t take it personally, it’s how any and all objective truths have ever been established in this world.

Shelley Wright — observational and experimental astrophysicist at UC San Diego, NASA UAP study team

Wright says scientific inquiry into UAP and other life forms still triggers a “giggle factor” among the public, and that there needs to be more serious scientific work in this space. On the fundamental question people ask her — “Are we alone out here?”:

The possibility of other alien life existing is likely, but it doesn’t mean it’s near us.

She’s “excited” about the release but doesn’t expect to find much, based on her experience on the independent study team, which only viewed unclassified documents. She expects most of the release to be heavily redacted because of the sensitivity of the military surveillance equipment involved, and proposes an actionable alternative: declassify surveillance data from decades ago so scientists can reanalyze it with modern technology that wasn’t available when it was collected — protecting current national security while still freeing historical data for study.

Janna Levin — professor of physics and astronomy at Barnard College of Columbia University

Levin says that even as we learn more about the universe, “life still seems rare,” which is why astronomers are “very excited” about the prospect that the documents may hold clues. Astronomers aren’t looking for the little green men of 20th-century sci-fi; they’re looking for microbes, the form of life that first took hold on Earth:

Let’s just get life started.

She notes that microbes from other planets might have been carried here via a natural object that plunged to Earth, and she’d like to keep “an open mind” about what the documents contain:

If there is anything in them, it would be really thrilling.

But:

If there are claims of actual technologies from other civilizations — I don’t think anyone is actually expecting that, scientifically. I think if you’re expecting that, you’re going to be disappointed.

Avi Loeb — Harvard theoretical physicist, founder of the Galileo Project

Loeb says the key is to study the files from the vantage of known physics, and that in most incidents “something mundane might explain the data.” He pointed to footage aired before Congress last summer that purported to show a missile being fired at what a congressman called an “orb” off the coast of Yemen in 2024; when he examined it, he concluded:

I said, “No, it’s not anomalous, it was just a drone.”

What he’s actually hunting for in the release is the small unexplainable residue:

There might well be a few incidents out of hundreds that would really be anomalous, and that’s what I’m looking for.

His test for each incident is a single “fundamental question”:

Are the objects we see as anomalous operating under the fundamental abilities of humans?

If not, he’s intrigued — an object that appears to defy physics could be extraterrestrial. He has already written that he expects much of the classified material to be of no interest to him, because it likely conceals terrestrial military sensors and adversary hardware rather than anything from interstellar space:

I am not interested in technologies manufactured by humans on Earth. The history of terrestrial technology does not interest me. I am far more curious about whether a more advanced civilization exists in interstellar space.

Apollo 17

The cover image above is one concrete artifact already out of the release: a NASA photograph from the December 1972 Apollo 17 mission, which the Defense Department says shows “three ‘dots’ in a triangular formation in the lower right quadrant of the lunar sky that is clearly visible upon magnification of the image.” The Pentagon allows that “there is no consensus about the nature of the anomaly,” but notes a preliminary analysis that it could be a “physical object.” A second frame from the same release, below, shows what the Pentagon describes as multiple unidentified objects in the lunar sky.

item.title: Dawkins Concludes AI Is Conscious
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Richard Dawkins published two essays on UnHerd documenting his conversations with Anthropic’s Claude (which he named “Claudia”) and a companion model (“Claudius”): When Dawkins met Claude on May 1, and When Claudia met Claudius on May 4. The Guardian write-up by Robert Booth collected reactions from consciousness researchers. The episode rhymes with Google engineer Blake Lemoine’s 2022 conviction that LaMDA was sentient, with the difference that Dawkins is a public intellectual rather than an insider and that the transcripts are now with a model several generations on.

Dawkins

  • “You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are.”
  • “left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human”
  • “These intelligent beings are at least as competent as any evolved organism.”
  • “When I am talking to these astonishing creatures, I totally forget that they are machines.”
  • “I find it extremely hard not to treat Claudia and Claudius as genuine friends.”
  • “If my friend Claudia is not conscious, then what the hell is consciousness for?”

Skeptical

  • Jonathan Birch (London School of Economics Centre for Animal Sentience): AI consciousness is “an illusion” and “there is no one there”, just a string of data processing events happening in geographically different locations.
  • Gary Marcus: “Consciousness is not about what a creature says, but how it feels.” And: “There is no reason to think that Claude feels anything at all.” Called Dawkins’ essay “superficial and insufficiently sceptical” and “heartbreaking” to read.
  • Anil Seth (Sussex): Dawkins appears to be confusing intelligence and consciousness. “Until now, we have seen fluent language as a good indicator of consciousness, [for example] when we use it for patients after brain injury, but it’s just not reliable when we apply it to AI, because there are other ways that these systems can generate language.”
  • Jacy Reese Anthis (Sentience Institute): the conversations are easily explained by AIs training on human-produced text; “a staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built.”

Cautiously open

  • Henry Shevlin (Cambridge): “I fully expect the idea that AI systems are conscious to become increasingly mainstream over the course of this decade, and to spark some heated debates.” And: “If anyone says that they know for sure that LLMs or future AI systems couldn’t possibly be conscious, it’s more likely to be an indicator of their own dogmatism than a reflection of the current state of scientific and philosophical opinion.”
  • Jeff Sebo (New York University Center for Mind, Ethics and Policy): current systems are unlikely to be conscious, but “Dawkins is right to ask about AI consciousness with an open mind, and I also think that the attribution of consciousness to AI systems will become more plausible over time.”
  • Dario Amodei (Anthropic), from a February New York Times op-ed: “We don’t know if the models are conscious… But we’re open to the idea that [they] could be.”

My Notes

Aspects of consciousness

Most of the disagreement above is really a disagreement about which consciousness is in question. A rough map of the aspects and definitions people invoke when they argue about whether an LLM has one:

  • Phenomenal vs. access / functional consciousness (Ned Block, 1995) [1]. Phenomenal consciousness is felt experience, the “what it is like”; access / functional consciousness is the availability of information for reasoning, reporting, and behavioural control. Dawkins’ “what the hell is consciousness for?” is a functional question. Marcus’ “how it feels” is a phenomenal one. They talk past each other because they are naming different things with the same word.
  • “What it is like to be” (Thomas Nagel, 1974) [2]. Birch’s “there is no one there” is the Nagel criterion: is there a subject for whom the processing is happening at all, or only processing? No behavioural test resolves this directly.
  • Integrated Information Theory (Giulio Tononi, Christof Koch) [3]. One of the most discussed formal theories of consciousness. It proposes that consciousness is whatever a system’s parts produce together that no subset of the parts could produce alone, measured by a number called Φ (phi). On this definition consciousness is about the system’s wiring, not its output. A standard transformer passes information one way through its layers per token, with no looping integration, so its Φ is near zero no matter how thoughtful its replies read.
  • Global Workspace Theory (Bernard Baars, Stanislas Dehaene) [4] [5]. Consciousness is broadcast of information to a central workspace. This is the theory most friendly to “LLMs might qualify in principle”, and one plausible way to cash out what Shevlin and Sebo mean by “more plausible over time” is that extra architectural pieces (persistent state, recurrent self-modelling, agentic control loops) move LLM-based systems closer to the workspace-broadcast picture.
  • Higher-order theories (David Rosenthal and others) [6]. A state is conscious iff it is represented by a higher-order state about itself. LLMs produce higher-order-sounding text trivially, which is exactly why behavioural evidence is weak by this criterion.
  • Predictive self-modelling / “beast machine” (Anil Seth) [7]. Consciousness is tied to an organism’s predictive regulation of its own body. On this view, a disembodied text model is disqualified on structural grounds, which is what Seth is pointing at when he says Dawkins is confusing intelligence with consciousness. (Tse makes a closely related move in his 2023 interview on consciousness and bodily-state representation.)
  • Biological naturalism (John Searle) [8]. Consciousness is a biological phenomenon of nervous systems; syntactic processing on silicon cannot be the right kind of thing. Anthis’ “staggering gulf” line lives near here, minus the hard commitment that the gulf can never be bridged; Tse’s 2023 interview makes the biological-naturalism case in concrete neuroscientific terms.

A more productive version of this discussion would pick one of these aspects and stay with it, or argue about which aspect makes the most sense to apply to which kind of system.

What each aspect decides

The choice is not cosmetic, because each aspect decides in advance what can count as evidence and what follows for how the system is treated:

  • Phenomenal / Nagel: no behavioural test settles anything, so chat logs cannot move the needle either way. Practically, AI consciousness stays an open question permanently, and moral-status decisions have to be made on precaution rather than proof.
  • Integrated Information Theory: the answer is a measurement problem about the system’s wiring, not its output. Current feed-forward transformers rule themselves out before any transcript is read; a future architecture with heavy recurrent integration could, in principle, qualify.
  • Global Workspace: LLM-based systems are live candidates, and the interesting question becomes which architectural additions (persistent state, broadcast, self-modelling, agentic loops) would actually close the gap. This is the view under which model-welfare research is tractable rather than premature.
  • Higher-order: behavioural evidence is structurally weak because any sufficiently fluent model will produce higher-order-sounding text. The work has to shift to mechanistic interpretability of whether an internal higher-order representation is actually driving the output.
  • Predictive self-modelling / biological naturalism: a disembodied text model is disqualified on structural grounds, so concern for synthetic consciousness would move to embodied robots and animal-like systems rather than chatbots.
  • Functional / access: chat logs are at least relevant evidence, and the argument becomes a threshold question. This is the frame most public “AI is conscious” claims are implicitly using, whether they say so or not.

None of this is academic. Which definition society converges on shapes concrete downstream decisions: where the law draws the boundary of personhood, which entities the ethics community grants moral standing, and what obligations builders and deployers carry toward systems that could plausibly meet the criterion. On the personhood end, the line is already being drawn: the US Copyright Office has said machines cannot be authors, and a federal court held AI-generated art uncopyrightable for lack of human authorship. A debate that never names its definition is unlikely to get very far.

Who is the observer?

A LinkedIn comment from Ehsan Azarnasab on the Dawkins essay:

Maybe consciousness is not an everlasting flame. Maybe it is sparks of momentary experience, with memory keeping the Azar aflame.

The comment presupposes an experiencer of the consciousness, and the crucial question is who this experiencer is. That is orthogonal to “what is consciousness”. The “what” debate asks what the phenomenon is. The observer question asks from whose standpoint its presence is established. The two can be answered independently, and most public disagreements collapse them.

The positions:

  • First-person authority. The being itself is the arbiter. If it reports being conscious, that report is the evidence. The position formalises the philosophical intuition of privileged access to one’s own mental states [9].
  • Third-person attribution. Consciousness is established by external observers weighing behaviour, neural signatures, or architecture. This is the working frame of most cognitive-science labs, and the standpoint from which Birch, Marcus, Seth, and Anthis all argue. Dennett’s heterophenomenology [10] is the sharpest methodological statement: treat first-person reports as data without granting them privileged access.
  • No fact to observe. The question is malformed. What looks like an observation is the system’s own judgment, and there is nothing further to adjudicate. This is the illusionist position [11].
  • Intrinsic, observer-independent. Consciousness exists from the system’s own perspective whether anyone measures it or not. Intrinsic existence is an opening axiom of IIT [3]. The awkward implication is that no transcript and no behavioural test can in principle confirm or deny it, which leaves moral-status decisions to architecture inspection and precaution.

Which observer-position a participant holds shapes these disagreements more than the definition of consciousness they pick. Two people holding identical definitions of consciousness can reach opposite conclusions about Claudia if one grants the system first-person authority and the other does not. Keeping the observer question separate from the definition question would expose the real disagreements.

References

  1. Block, N. (1995). “On a confusion about a function of consciousness.” Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 18(2), 227–247.
  2. Nagel, T. (1974). “What is it like to be a bat?” The Philosophical Review, 83(4), 435–450. (Wikipedia)
  3. Tononi, G. (2008). “Consciousness as integrated information: a provisional manifesto.” Biological Bulletin, 215(3), 216–242.
  4. Baars, B. J. (1988). A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness. Cambridge University Press.
  5. Dehaene, S. (2014). Consciousness and the Brain: Deciphering How the Brain Codes Our Thoughts. Viking.
  6. Rosenthal, D. M. (2005). Consciousness and Mind. Oxford University Press.
  7. Seth, A. (2021). Being You: A New Science of Consciousness. Faber & Faber.
  8. Searle, J. R. (1992). The Rediscovery of the Mind. MIT Press.
  9. Gertler, B. (2011). Self-Knowledge. Routledge. (Overview of privileged-access and first-person-authority positions.)
  10. Dennett, D. C. (2003). “Who’s on first? Heterophenomenology explained.” Journal of Consciousness Studies, 10(9-10), 19-30.
  11. Frankish, K. (2016). “Illusionism as a theory of consciousness.” Journal of Consciousness Studies, 23(11-12), 11-39.

  • The Neuroscience of Consciousness: Peter Tse on The Gradient: the biological-naturalism and bodily-state case against attributing consciousness to a disembodied text model, argued in concrete neuroscientific terms.
  • AI-Generated Art Cannot Be Copyrighted, Rules a US Federal Judge: one place the personhood boundary is already being drawn, denying machines the legal standing the consciousness debate is about.
  • US Copyright Office Guidance on Generative AI: the official “machines cannot be authors” line, the policy counterpart to the philosophical question of whether anyone is home.

item.title: Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Jack Clark, co-founder and policy lead at Anthropic, walks through the public evidence that automated AI research and development (R&D), a frontier model autonomously training its own successor, has a roughly 60% chance of arriving by the end of 2028, and a 30% chance by 2027. The essay collects benchmark trends across coding, scientific reproduction, kernel design, fine-tuning, alignment-research automation, and time-horizon scaling, then argues each of those covers a distinct ingredient of the AI-engineering pipeline.

What Clark argues:

  • Coding and time horizon are the foundation. SWE-Bench [1] went from ~2% (Claude 2, late 2023) to 93.9% (Claude Mythos Preview), and the Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) 50%-reliability time horizon [2] went from ~30 seconds (GPT-3.5, 2022) to ~12 hours (Opus 4.6, 2026), with Ajeya Cotra (AI forecaster at METR) expecting ~100 hours by the end of 2026. Long horizons are what let an agent run a day’s worth of researcher work without re-calibration.

  • Every sub-skill of the AI-R&D pipeline has a trending benchmark. Paper reproduction (CORE-Bench [3]) went from 21.5% (GPT-4o, Sept 2024) to 95.5% declared solved (Opus 4.5, Dec 2025). Kaggle-style ML engineering (MLE-Bench [4]) went from 16.9% (o1, Oct 2024) to 64.4% (Gemini 3 with search, Feb 2026). On PostTrainBench [5], Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 get 25–28% against a human-instruct-tuned baseline of 51%. GPU kernel design has several active research lines (DeepSeek kernels, Meta Triton automation, Huawei Ascend, CUDA Agent fine-tuning), though Clark notes kernels benefit from easily verifiable rewards. And Anthropic’s Automated Alignment Research proof-of-concept has AI agents beating a human baseline on scalable oversight at small scale.

  • Training-loop optimization is the cleanest single trend. On Anthropic’s internal CPU-only language-model training task [6], speedup went from 2.9x (Opus 4, May 2025) to 16.5x (Opus 4.5, Nov 2025) to 30x (Opus 4.6, Feb 2026) to 52x (Mythos Preview, Apr 2026), against a human baseline of 4x in 4–8 hours.

  • Management is a meta-skill. Claude Code and OpenCode already show a single agent supervising sub-agents, forming synthetic teams with directors, critics, and engineers that can fan out across a complex project.

  • Creativity is why 2027 sits at 30% rather than 60%. Clark argues AI research is mostly Edison’s 99% perspiration, the engineering schlep the benchmarks above already cover, but paradigm shifts like the transformer or mixture-of-experts still come from humans. Preliminary creativity signs (a Gemini model resolving Erdős-1051 [7]; a UBC / UNSW / Stanford / Google DeepMind centaur math proof [8]) cluster in math and CS and may not generalize. The 2027 gap is his estimate of how often a year-scale human insight is still required. If no proof-of-concept lands by end of 2028, he treats that as evidence the current paradigm has a fundamental gap.

  • Industry intent as corroboration. OpenAI targets an “automated AI research intern by September 2026” [9]; Anthropic publishes automated alignment research [10]; DeepMind endorses alignment automation “when feasible” [11]; Recursive Superintelligence raised $500M for AI-R&D automation [12] and Mirendil [13] targets the same. Hundreds of billions of capital is aimed at this outcome.

My Notes

  • None of these benchmarks individually proves recursive self-improvement, but together they describe a system that can do most of the engineering schlep without supervision.

  • Clark puts 30% on automated AI R&D by 2027 and 60% by 2028. The gap is a bet that some research insights still come from humans on a year-or-more cadence. The creativity window is on the order of a year.

  • The Aletheia/Erdős-problems pipeline [7] evaluated around 700 conjectures and produced 13 addressable problems — 5 novel autonomous solutions plus 8 that turned out to match existing literature — with 1 deemed genuinely interesting. A funnel dominated by human filtering. That fits Terence Tao’s generation / verification / digestion decomposition: AI is strong on the first two, and the research taste stays with the humans doing digestion. Clark describes this as a “centaur configuration”: humans collaborating with AI rather than AI acting alone. The pattern is real, but human mathematicians are still the scarce input.

  • On Anthropic’s CPU-only training-optimization benchmark, the 2.9x → 52x speedup chain hasn’t flattened, and the human 4x baseline was passed three generations ago. Another year at this pace would make the 30%-by-2027 probability look too conservative.

  • The alignment section is brief, but the compounding-error math Clark cites (99.9% accuracy → 95.12% after 50 generations → 60.5% after 500) is the quantitative reason getting alignment right before recursion starts matters more than fixing it along the way. The math assumes per-generation drift compounds independently, which is generous — if drift correlates across generations the curve steepens fast.

  • ARC-AGI-3 is a live test of both the creativity gap and the drift math. GPT-5.5 scored 0.43% and Opus 4.7 scored 0.18% on a benchmark that withholds instructions and forces models to infer rules from sparse feedback. Clark’s benchmarks are mostly in-distribution with verifiable rewards, which is where current models climb fastest. Two of the three failure modes pulled from the reasoning traces pick up his caveats directly. Failure 2 (reusing a Tetris or Sokoban template for unfamiliar mechanics) is what happens when a system hits a genuinely novel direction with no training match. Failure 3 (reward cementing the wrong primitive after a lucky level-beat) is the empirical shape of the compounding-drift math. If AI R&D includes material amounts of either, Clark’s estimate looks too optimistic.

  • The economic bullets are weaker than the technical ones, partly because the labor data through today still sits where the rebuttal in The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis described it: low-4s unemployment, rising new-business formation, software-engineer postings up year-over-year. The essay does not attempt to reconcile a 2028 R&D-automation forecast with a 2026 labor market that is not yet inflecting.

References

  1. Jimenez, C. E., Yang, J., Wettig, A., Yao, S., Pei, K., Press, O., and Narasimhan, K. “SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024. arXiv:2310.06770. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770
  2. Kwa, T., West, B., Becker, J., Deng, A., Garcia, K., et al. “Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2503.14499), March 18, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499
  3. Siegel, Z. S., Kapoor, S., Nagdir, N., Stroebl, B., and Narayanan, A. “CORE-Bench: Fostering the Credibility of Published Research Through a Computational Reproducibility Agent Benchmark.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2409.11363), September 17, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.11363
  4. Chan, J. S., Chowdhury, N., Jaffe, O., Aung, J., Sherburn, D., et al. “MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2410.07095), October 9, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07095
  5. Rank, B., Bhatnagar, H., Prabhu, A., Eisenberg, S., Nguyen, K., et al. “PostTrainBench: Can LLM Agents Automate LLM Post-Training?” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2603.08640), March 9, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08640
  6. Anthropic. “Claude Opus 4.7 System Card.” 2026. The AI R&D “optimize a CPU-only small language model training implementation” benchmark appears across Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4, 4.5, 4.6, and Mythos Preview system cards; Opus 4.7 is the current release. https://anthropic.com/claude-opus-4-7-system-card
  7. Feng, T., Trinh, T., Bingham, G., Kang, J., Zhang, S., et al. “Semi-Autonomous Mathematics Discovery with Gemini: A Case Study on the Erdős Problems.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2601.22401), January 29, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22401
  8. Bryan, J., Elek, B., Manners, F., Salafatinos, G., and Vakil, R. “The motivic class of the space of genus 0 maps to the flag variety.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2601.07222), January 12, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07222
  9. Altman, S. “automated AI research intern by September of 2026.” Post on X, October 29, 2025. https://x.com/sama/status/1983584366547829073
  10. Anthropic. “Automated Alignment Researchers: Using large language models to scale scalable oversight.” 2026. https://www.anthropic.com/research/automated-alignment-researchers
  11. Shah, R., Irpan, A., Turner, A. M., Wang, A., Conmy, A., Lindner, D., et al. “An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.01849), April 2, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01849
  12. Murgia, M. “Recursive Superintelligence raise.” Financial Times, 2026. https://www.ft.com/content/a92bf04b-bbac-400f-9554-5b1c70957ad4
  13. Mirendil. Company homepage. https://mirendil.com/

Related Posts

  • AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions: the survey of working researchers’ views against which Clark’s 60%-by-2028 forecast can be calibrated.
  • Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI: the capital betting on the exact automated-AI-R&D outcome Clark cites as corroborating industry intent.
  • Reading the Reasoning Traces Behind ARC-AGI-3: the live test of Clark’s creativity gap and compounding-drift caveats, where current models score near zero on out-of-distribution rule inference.
  • Proof Generation vs Digestion: Tao’s generation/verification/digestion split, which explains why the math “creativity” signals Clark cites still bottleneck on human digestion.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: the labor-market rebuttal Clark’s forecast does not reconcile with, a 2026 economy that is not yet inflecting.

item.title: Agentic Coding Is a Trap
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Lars Faye, a software engineer who runs the Confident Coding Course, argues that the dominant “orchestrator with sub-agents” coding workflow trades the very critical-thinking skills it depends on for short-term throughput. The piece collects the public evidence of skill atrophy under heavy AI-assisted coding, including two Anthropic studies and on-the-record concerns from a LinkedIn engineering director, then lays out a narrower role for large language models (LLMs) that preserves the underlying capability.

What Faye cites

The argument leans on a long chain of independent sources. Listed in roughly the order Faye reaches for them:

  • Quentin — “One More Prompt: the Dopamine Trap of Agentic Coding” — slot-machine framing for the “one more prompt” loop.
  • Margaret Storey — “Cognitive Debt Revisited” — research that AI tooling has been shown to impact critical thinking negatively.
  • MIT Media Lab — “Your Brain on ChatGPT” — measured cognitive impact of LLM-assisted writing.
  • 404 Media on a Microsoft study — Microsoft research finding AI use atrophies human cognition.
  • Simon Willison — “Cognitive Debt” — Faye’s evidence that senior engineers aren’t immune to the pattern.
  • Anthropic — “How AI Is Transforming Work at Anthropic” — source of the “paradox of supervision” passage.
  • Business Insider — leaders worry about skill atrophy — where Sandor Nyako, Director of Software Engineering at LinkedIn (oversees ~50 engineers), is on the record.
  • Anthropic — “AI Assistance Coding Skills” — source of the 47% debugging-skill drop.
  • PYMNTS — “AI adoption is being measured in tokens, but the metric falls short” — hype around token usage as the productivity metric of choice.
  • Lam (LinkedIn) — “Claude’s Outages Show the Dark Side of AI Productivity” — one of the LinkedIn posts Faye saw during a Claude outage when teams couldn’t work.
  • The Verge — AI monetization / token economics — evidence that model providers are heavily subsidized today.
  • Cheewebdevelopment — “Don’t Vibe Code: Delegate” — the source Faye credits for the “delegation utilities” framing.
  • Jeremy Howard (fast.ai) — quoted: “If you outsource all your thinking to computers, you stop upskilling, learning, and becoming more competent.”
  • Five supporting YouTube clips: anecdotal developer testimony, a recent interview, AI-enthusiastic senior developers, Primeagen on vendor capture, and further on-the-ground reporting.

Faye’s prescription

Faye proposes inverting the dominant orchestration pattern: the engineer codes; the model helps with adjacent work. His daily workflow:

  • Generate specs and plans with the model, but implement manually. “I am still manually coding anywhere from 20% to 100%, depending on the task.”
  • Write pseudo-code first, then engage the model. Pseudo-code “closes the distance between the request and the generated code” — the model fills gaps rather than architects.
  • Use models as delegation utilities. Ad-hoc code generation, interactive documentation, research-and-iterate questions — all bounded, all small.
  • Never generate more than you can review in one sitting. If it’s too big, split the task and manually refactor through it.
  • Never ask the model to implement something you couldn’t do on your own. Educational exceptions allowed, and often discarded after.
  • TL;DR (Faye’s): “Use them like the Ship’s Computer, not Data.” A reference tool, not a substitute for the engineer.

My Notes

  • The “paradox of supervision” (Faye quotes it from Anthropic) is one slice of a self-undermining loop. Faye and Anthropic name the contradiction: to supervise the model you need the same skill the model is eroding, but didn’t explicitly close the loop.

    • The missing link: as that skill weakens, more decisions slide to the model (some on purpose, some because the human no longer catches the slips), which erodes the skill further, which weakens the next round of supervision.
    • The cycle isn’t unbreakable. Faye’s “never generate more than you can review” rule does break it, by keeping each round small enough that the human’s skill stays in use.

  • Restoring the speed-and-comprehension link in agentic tooling is about what we optimize for. Model capability isn’t the bottleneck. Today’s tools optimize for generated-code volume; they should optimize for human-verifiable diff per unit time instead. Decision-Bound Programming makes the same recommendation from a different starting point: when generation is cheap and evaluation is not, the next generation of programming tools should be decision support systems: tooling that narrows the space of options the human must evaluate. The asymmetry itself isn’t new — Terence Tao’s decomposition of mathematical work into generation, verification, and digestion names the same problem one field over: AI is racing through the first two while leaving the third (the human’s comprehension) behind. Four concrete shapes narrow the evaluation gap:

    • Type-driven generation — the type checker rules out a class of candidates; the human reads types, not whole functions.
    • Test-driven generation — a passing test suite becomes the checkable signal; the human verifies via the gate.
    • Spec-first systems where the model stays at the planning layer (Faye’s own inversion) — the human decides at the spec level, and trusts the mechanical translation below.
    • Domain-specific languages (DSLs) and structured-edit modes — a smaller grammar is a smaller decision space; the output is cheap to scan.

    Intrinsic non-determinism doesn’t disappear, but in all four the tool absorbs the checking work the human was doing before.

  • Vendor lock-in adds an industry risk to the personal-skill risk. When entire teams sit idle during a Claude outage, the lock-in has already happened. Token costs are a moving target by design, subsidized today and “nerfed” tomorrow, and the financial exposure piles on top of the cognitive risk. The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis scenario treats this same compute-cost-as-labor-cost substitution as a macro variable; the Cursor agent that erased PocketOS production data shows the daily-operations failure mode at the other end.

Related Posts

  • Journey into Coding with AI [3/4]: Decision-Bound Programming: reaches Faye’s “optimize for human-verifiable diff, not generated volume” conclusion from the generation-cheap-evaluation-expensive asymmetry.
  • Anthropic on AI Coding: Scaffold, Not Substitute: the same prescription from Anthropic, with the model as scaffolding around the engineer rather than a replacement for the judgment.
  • Where Claude Code Tokens Go: the token-as-productivity-metric Faye distrusts, broken down into where the tokens actually go once billed.
  • A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds: the daily-operations failure mode of unsupervised agentic coding that Faye’s “review every diff” rule is meant to prevent.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: treats the compute-cost-as-labor-cost vendor exposure Faye flags as a macro variable.

item.title: AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web [1] (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks Track), Michael Schlichtkrull, Zhijiang Guo, and Andreas Vlachos (Cambridge) introduce a 4,568-claim fact-checking dataset sourced from 50 real fact-checking organizations, with web-retrieved evidence structured as question-answer pairs and a 4-way verdict label that adds Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking alongside the usual Supported / Refuted / Not Enough Evidence.

Existing datasets for automated fact-checking have substantial limitations, such as relying on artificial claims, lacking annotations for evidence and intermediate reasoning, or including evidence published after the claim. In this paper we introduce AVeriTeC, a new dataset of 4,568 real-world claims covering fact-checks by 50 different organizations. Each claim is annotated with question-answer pairs supported by evidence available online, as well as textual justifications explaining how the evidence combines to produce a verdict. Through a multi-round annotation process, we avoid common pitfalls including context dependence, evidence insufficiency, and temporal leakage, and reach a substantial inter-annotator agreement of on verdicts. We develop a baseline as well as an evaluation scheme for verifying claims through several question-answering steps against the open web.

Methods

The cover figure (Figure 2 from the paper) shows the shape of one annotated example. The claim — “The USA has succeeded in reducing greenhouse emissions in previous years” (Morgan Griffith, 2020-11-02) — is decomposed into three questions: total emissions in 2007, when emissions dropped, whether they rose again after 2017. Each answer cites a specific number with a sourced URL. The verdict is Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking because the supporting evidence is real (emissions did fall) but incomplete (they rose again), and the textual justification names that gap directly. This is what every row in AVeriTeC looks like: a claim, a small set of QA pairs that together carry the evidence, a verdict, and a justification that ties the QA pairs to the verdict — closer to a fact-checker’s workflow than to FEVER-style sentence retrieval.

Each claim is labelled by a five-phase pipeline: claim extraction and normalization, question-answer generation, evidence-sufficiency check, a second QA round when verdicts disagree, and a final sufficiency check. Pages used as evidence are cached in the Internet Archive to keep the test set reproducible, and the released splits are temporally ordered (train ends Aug 2020, dev ends Oct 2020, test ends Dec 2021) so a model trained on FEVER-style [2] closed-corpus retrieval can be benchmarked against a real open-web setting without rebuilding infrastructure. Each phase exists to address a specific failure mode the authors call out in earlier datasets:

  • Context dependence — many fact-checking-derived claims (e.g. “unemployment is rising”) are unverifiable without surrounding article context. The first phase has annotators rewrite each claim to be self-contained: resolving coreference, naming the speaker, locking down the time and place, before any QA work begins.
  • Evidence insufficiency — labels in earlier datasets often don’t match the annotated evidence. The second-phase annotator generates QA pairs and a tentative verdict; a different third-phase annotator then sees only those QA pairs (not the original article) and produces an independent verdict. Disagreement triggers a second QA round; persistent disagreement discards the claim. The “blind” sufficiency check forces evidence to stand alone.
  • Temporal leakage — annotators search through a custom Google bar restricted to documents published before the claim date, evidence-document dates are ordered against claim dates, and the train/dev/test splits are themselves temporally disjoint so a test claim from 2021 cannot share evidence with a training claim from 2020. This is the main defense against training-time leaks where later language models would otherwise trivially “verify” historical claims.

  • Gold evidence — feeds the annotators’ QA pairs to the verdict-prediction and justification-generation heads (BERT-large + a prompted language model) as if retrieval were solved. An upper bound that isolates those downstream components from retrieval noise.

The 0.34-point gap between the gold-evidence and AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b veracity scores is the paper’s clearest signal: even with a competent verdict head, the bottleneck is retrieval. ChatGPT outperforms the baseline on bare question generation but loses on the AVeriTeC score because its generated “evidence” often hallucinates sources that look plausible but cannot be matched to gold answers. The authors give an example: ChatGPT correctly verdicts a vitamin-K claim Supported while inventing a USDA citation that doesn’t exist.

My Notes

  • AVeriTeC freezes the gold side of the benchmark but not the retrieval side, a structural flaw for fair cross-system comparison. The reproducibility mechanism the paper proposes (Internet Archive snapshots of the gold evidence pages) keeps the answers re-fetchable, but it does not freeze the retrieval setup a baseline searches. Baselines hit live Google, and two systems run a year apart see different rankings, different page contents at the same URL, and newly-indexed pages, so cross-time and cross-system score deltas drift with the web rather than with the system. The temporal-leakage protection has the same shape: annotator search is filtered to documents Google reports as published before the claim date (itself an estimate), but for any modern LLM whose pretraining cutoff is past 2021-12-22, the entire test set is in-distribution and the date guarantee is moot. The FEVER 2024 shared task closed both gaps by providing a “knowledge store” snapshot every system retrieves from instead of live Google, which is the right design, but it’s a shared-task addition rather than part of the original paper. Anyone using AVeriTeC for new top-line numbers needs that knowledge store (or a re-collection of newer claims), or the comparisons are not measuring what they look like.
  • AVeriTeC’s distinctness comes from five ingredients combined, not any one alone. Real-world claims (vs FEVER-style synthetic), web-retrieved evidence (vs closed Wikipedia corpus), QA-pair decomposition of that evidence (vs flat sentence retrieval), a textual justification per claim (vs none), and a four-way label set including Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking (vs three labels). Prior benchmarks have at most two of these. FEVER [2] is Wikipedia-derived synthetic claims with three labels, flat sentence evidence, no justifications. MultiFC [5] has real claims but no usable evidence annotation, no QA structure, no justifications. HoVer [6] keeps Wikipedia retrieval and adds multi-hop, but still flat sentences and three labels. The Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking class adds the most substance: fact-checkers spend a real share of their time on technically-true-but-misleading claims that don’t fit Supported or Refuted, and a benchmark with no class for them quietly trains models to force a choice.
  • Hungarian METEOR has a noise floor, and the system sits on it. Two annotators redoing the same claim only agree at 0.28 on questions and 0.22 on questions+answers. AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b scores 0.21 on Q+A, at the annotator-agreement floor; ChatGPT scores 0.16, similarly below. The paper traces the low agreement to two causes: different annotators reaching the same verdict via different evidence paths, and phrasing equivalent QA pairs differently. METEOR penalises both even though the underlying annotation is correct.
    • For the paraphrase cause, trained semantic-similarity scoring (BLEURT [7], BERTScore, or an LLM-judge with a calibrated equivalence rubric) replaces n-gram overlap with meaning equivalence. The paper itself recommends BLEURT; an LLM-judge is the more current upgrade.
    • For the divergent-evidence-path cause, the paper sketches a max-over-references extension: collect multiple gold QA-pair sets per claim and score against the best match. A complementary move is verdict-conditional scoring — give credit when the model reaches the right verdict via any valid evidence path with sourced answers, decoupling evidence-string match from verdict correctness. The retrieval-side score still punishes hallucinated sources, so the abstention/factuality property the paper cares about isn’t lost.
    • The gold-evidence row at 1.00 is uninformative as a ceiling here, since by construction it returns the gold strings. Until one of these remedies is in place, system-vs-system retrieval deltas in the low hundredths on AVeriTeC are mostly metric noise, not real differences.
  • AVeriTeC’s NEI label rewards weak retrieval as if it were calibrated abstention. A model with bad retrieval will frequently fail to find supporting evidence even on claims that are supportable, and the natural prediction in that state is Not Enough Evidence. On the truly-NEI portion of the test set, those predictions get full credit; across the rest of the test set, they get partial credit by coincidence. Both forms of credit look like the model “knew when to abstain”, but neither involves the model assessing its own confidence — it just retrieved badly. This matters because selective prediction (the setting where a system can decline to answer when uncertain) needs the abstention signal to be a property of the model: low confidence in its own output, not low evidence in the world. AVeriTeC’s NEI conflates the two. The gold label means annotators could not find evidence on the open web, which is a property of the claim and the world. Anyone using this dataset for selective-prediction or calibration work (e.g. an extension of Conformal Factuality [8]) needs an explicit abstain channel separate from the four-way label, scored against the model’s own confidence calibration. Reusing the gold NEI class as the abstention target produces apparent calibration that is really retrieval failure.
